title: The Reader's Share of Meaning
text:
Formalist critics of the early twentieth century argued that a literary work should be studied as a self-contained object, independent of its author's biography or historical circumstances. They focused on ambiguity, irony, and the tension between form and content, insisting that meaning emerges from the internal relations among words rather than from any external source. Such a view, however, invited the objection that the reader's own interpretive activity was being quietly excluded from the analysis.

Reader-response theorists later challenged this austerity by placing the reader at the centre of meaning-making. For them, a text remains indeterminate until it is actualised by a particular reader whose expectations and experiences shape what is perceived. The shift provoked considerable debate, since critics feared that interpretation might dissolve into mere subjective preference. Nevertheless, the movement permanently altered how scholars understand the relationship between a text and its audience.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, how did formalist critics argue that a literary work should be studied?
options: As a self-contained object, independent of its author's biography
As a historical record of social change
As a psychological portrait of its author
As a collection of moral lessons

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, when does a text become actualised?
options: When a particular reader engages with it
When critics agree on its meaning

questions.text: What can be inferred about the objection raised against formalist criticism?
options: It suggests that formalism overlooks the role of the reader in interpretation
It shows that formalists rejected close reading entirely
It proves that the author's intention is always decisive
It argues that historical context is the only valid source of meaning

questions.text: What is the author's most likely attitude toward reader-response theory?
options: Dismissive, because it merely repeats formalist ideas
Qualifiedly appreciative, acknowledging both its controversy and its lasting influence
Hostile, because it makes all interpretation impossible
Indifferent, because it has had no measurable impact

paragraph_translations: Os críticos formalistas do início do século XX defendiam que uma obra literária deveria ser estudada como um objeto autocontido, independente da biografia de seu autor ou das circunstâncias históricas. Eles se concentravam na ambiguidade, na ironia e na tensão entre forma e conteúdo, insistindo que o sentido emerge das relações internas entre as palavras, e não de qualquer fonte externa. No entanto, essa visão suscitava a objeção de que a atividade interpretativa do leitor estava sendo silenciosamente excluída da análise.

Os teóricos da resposta do leitor desafiaram depois essa austeridade ao colocar o leitor no centro da construção do sentido. Para eles, um texto permanece indeterminado até ser atualizado por um leitor particular, cujas expectativas e experiências moldam o que é percebido. A mudança provocou considerável debate, pois os críticos temiam que a interpretação se dissolvesse em mera preferência subjetiva. Ainda assim, o movimento alterou de forma permanente a maneira como os estudiosos compreendem a relação entre um texto e seu público.
